I agree with this completely.

I was also banned recently. In the past, this kind of content was not considered a problem, but lately bans are being issued suddenly without any warning or explanation.

On top of that, having monetization revoked at the same time feels excessive. It honestly feels like this approach is only accelerating the loss of creators and users from the platform.

If creators always have to worry about being banned without notice, it becomes difficult to feel motivated to continue making content.

"Are world creators expected to accept the risk of being banned just for creating worlds?"

I agree, VRChat has no content without the efforts of world creators. If someone with a clean record has never made a mistake before, why be so harsh? The goal should be to correct what ever they are not happy with, not find a reason to ban.

I understand that the risk of a ban is a deterrent to people who might add something bad to a world, but people with obviously bad intentions are different from a first time or light offense. Mitigating factors are important and should be considered. Escalating factors exist too, of course.

I THINK THE RECENT VRCHAT MODERATION TEAM IS REALLY LOSING ITS MIND

I thought that the reason was the reason for the definition of "a gathering place to seek sexual connection" after receiving the deletion and ban of the matching world made by Mr. Jonipon, which has been a hot topic recently.

However, from the guidelines, it is a gray zone and the definition area is vague, so I thought that the definition should be clearer even if it is moderated.

However, in this "眉間を壊すチルワールド", the purpose is not "a gathering place for seeking sexual connection", but does not contain any sources that are subject to moderation.

It's not a content worth moderating at all

As a result, it may have become a place like the above definition...

If that's the case

The behavior and public opinion of the join user will lead to the moderation of the world producer.

In the event of unauthorized sexual expression within the group, etc., there are cases where the person in charge of the group is subject to moderation, but it is not specified that the world producer is responsible for it.

In other words, it is very likely that this moderation is unfair.

If the objection to the above is rejected, we will lose more trust in VRCHAT operation.

I wish you good luck

The recent issue of world deletions has become extremely serious, and I completely understand why you see it as a major concern. It is undeniably jarring and disheartening to see worlds that feature various expressions—which had been tolerated until now—suddenly disappear without any prior warning. Looking at the traces of missing worlds in one's favorites list day after day leaves a lingering sense of sadness. Even if the vanished worlds contained some form of sexual content or highly niche expressions, they were not forcing it upon the general public, and the majority of them could hardly be classified as explicit nudity.

In the first place, what is the purpose of the 18+ age verification method provided in this game? Instead of resorting to outright elimination, shouldn't isolation be the proper approach?

Regarding the specific world in question this time, it contained practically none of the aforementioned sexual elements. The only notable feature was a pen that makes sounds. If the moderation is strict enough to regulate a world like this, wouldn't it be far better for the community to handle malicious stickers and toxic users instead?

Furthermore, despite the near-total absence of sexual content in this instance, the enforcement went beyond just deleting the world; it also resulted in a short-term ban for the user.

To be completely honest, isn't that an overreaction?

Did he use a crasher avatar in a public instance? Not at all.

It is difficult to agree with the excessive exclusion of such communities. At the same time, I am not asking for them to be forced upon everyone. I simply believe that there should be a place where we can coexist in an isolated format—separate from those who cannot tolerate such subcultures or where it might be deemed inappropriate for younger audiences.

I am concerned that recent moderation may unintentionally remove the very spaces that made VRChat meaningful to many queer and subcultural users.

Protecting users from harassment and non-consensual exposure is important. But as feminist anthropologist Gayle Rubin argued in her work on sexual hierarchies, broad sexual regulation often does not simply target harm itself. It can mark non-normative sexual cultures as social risks and push marginal communities out first.

Queer theorist and public-sphere scholar Michael Warner also described queer “counterpublics” as spaces where people outside dominant norms can gather and become socially visible on their own terms.

For many people, VRChat has served as that kind of counterpublic. It has not merely been a neutral public square. It has also been a place where queer people, gender-nonconforming people, and niche subcultures could exist without being forced into the standards of the majority.

If moderation removes worlds without warning and also bans creators without clear explanation, creators will not know how to comply. More importantly, marginalized communities will learn that their spaces are tolerated only until they become visible.

I am not asking VRChat to allow everything everywhere. I am asking for clearer rules, warnings, age-gated separation where appropriate, and moderation that distinguishes harmful behavior from minority expression.

I share the same concerns, but I am against moving toward establishing more explicit rules (and I also think it would be difficult to achieve in practice).

I believe improving moderation practices instead — such as notifications and reviewing internal guidelines — would be a better approach.

運用の改善（通知や内部基準の見直し）がより良いと思います。

I agree with the core concern raised here.

VRChat's own Community Guidelines already define a clear boundary for zero-tolerance enforcement: CSAM, CSEA, non-consensual intimate imagery, credible threats of real-world violence, and terrorist content. These are the cases where an immediate, permanent ban is justified — because the harm is severe and irreversible.

But for violations that fall outside that narrow category, the current practice of issuing immediate bans without warning appears inconsistent with that same document, which otherwise grants enforcement on a "case-by-case basis." If the guidelines themselves distinguish between levels of severity, the enforcement process should reflect that too.

A widely referenced standard for community enforcement — the Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct — describes what it calls an "enforcement ladder": starting with a private warning, then temporary restrictions, then suspension with conditions for return, and only as a last resort, a permanent ban. The key principle is that bans should be "rarely used" and "only resorted to if working through other remedies has failed." The purpose of enforcement is to bring people back into compliance, not to expel them from the community.

I'm not suggesting VRChat adopt the Contributor Covenant wholesale. But the underlying principle — that enforcement should be corrective before it is punitive — seems like a reasonable standard to hold any community platform to. A tiered warning system for non-zero-tolerance violations would be a meaningful step in that direction.

> Are world creators expected to accept the risk of being banned just for creating worlds?

I think the system would be defeated if there are no penalties for the offender after harm to another person has been caused and reviewed by a moderator team, so a ban on first offense is appropriate. It's the important responsibility of the creator to make sure the content is compliant with [Creator Guidelines](https://hello.vrchat.com/creator-guidelines) before any harm is caused.

In this scenario, as you @{64e62a75627a906cc10a07b1|full_name}, I would suggest to remove the provocative content such as the cross with wristlocks on the wall (BDSM themes) and the few objects on the wall which look like sex toys (anal beads) from your (now removed) public world.

@{68098a4626271974ef4d2775|full_name} 

If I knew what the issue was, I could remove that part and re-upload the world. The problem is that no reason was given at all, and the ban was applied immediately.

Looking back on it now, I can understand that there may have been some elements that could be seen as risky. However, at the time, I genuinely thought they were not a problem. For example, the cross was intended as a Christian motif.

I heard that in the past, worlds were reviewed by the staff before moving from Labs to Public, but that no longer seems to be the case. I was not doing anything malicious, such as hiding prohibited items. Under a proper public review system, the world should have simply failed the review without the creator receiving a penalty.

Because of that, I feel that an immediate ban is excessive. For the sake of future creators as well, I think worlds should either be reviewed before becoming public, or at least receive a warning first instead of an instant ban.

Otherwise, it would become possible to ban creators based on only one part of almost any world.

Sorry for using machine translation.

@{64e62a75627a906cc10a07b1|full_name} 

> If I knew what the issue was, I could remove that part and re-upload the world.

I will quote it for you from the Creator Guidelines.

> Worlds containing “inflammatory” content may not be published to Community Labs or Public status.

> This means things like controversial topics, sensitive, intimate, or provocative content, or extreme horror or “shock” content.

It didn't take me longer than two minutes to find provocative content from a video clip showcasing your world. I suggest due diligence of following the Creator Guidelines in the future.

If the world SDK does not contain any reference to warranting the world follows the Creator Guidelines, I think that notice with a link to the Creator Guidelines should be added to the world SDK upload dialog.

details:
My world was banned, but why does that also come with a three-day user ban without any prior warning?

Simply removing a world and banning the user without explaining the reason makes it look like negligence on the staff’s part.

I have also heard that decisions are made based only on the contents of reports, but are these cases really being reviewed properly?

At the very least, I think there should be a warning first.

Are world creators expected to accept the risk of being banned just for creating worlds? There may be updates for other worlds, events to host, or events to attend, and preventing all of that feels like an excessive burden being placed on players.

If this situation does not improve, then as a creator, I will hesitate to continue making content at all.
title: Being Banned Without Warning Is Really Unfair
